newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea probes senior economic officials over Hanbo.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea probes senior economic officials over Hanbo.

text.p: South Korean state prosecutors said on Friday they were probing allegations that senior economic officials were involved in the collapse of failed Hanbo Steel Co.

Senior prosecutor Choi Hwan said the prosecution was determined to bring to justice all suspects in addition to the 10 people, including a former cabinet minister and close aides of President Kim Young-sam, already standing trial.

"We have been investigating the chief presidential economic adviser's office, the ministry of Finance and Economy and the Office of Bank Supervision to establish the truth over suspicions that they were involved in the process of handling Hanbo's defaults," he told a televised parliamentary hearing.

Prosecutors had also probed allegations that the president's second son, Kim Hyun-chul, accepted kickbacks and pressured banks to offer loans to Hanbo, but were unable to find any evidence implicating him, Choi said.
"We will continue to probe various allegations raised by the National Assembly and media, including those that Mr Kim Hyun-chul meddled in state affairs and that he accepted money."
Opposition members of parliament accused Hyun-chul of accepting a 200 billion won ($223 million) kickback from a businessman acting as an agent for Hanbo.
Hanbo Steel, South Korea's second largest steelmaker and flagship of the nation's 14th largest conglomerate, folded under debts of $5.8 billion.
South Korea's new finance minister, Kang Kyong-shik, acknowledged on Thursday that the economy was in serious trouble, battered by a trade deficit, labour unrest, bankruptcies and a political crisis.
Last week, Hanbo Group chairman Chung Bo-keun was arrested on charges of pocketing about 37 billion won from company funds.
Chung's father, Hanbo founder Chung Tae-soo, is among the 10 standing trial in connection with the loans scandal.
Prosecutor-general Kim Ki-soo told the hearing that the scandal had "enormously shocked" the nation. "We are exerting ourselves to end all suspicions over Hanbo," he said.
Hanbo Steel's failure revealed a web of corruption and influence-peddling that allowed the company to secure loans far in excess of its ability to repay them.

The chief prosecutor said the Hanbo founder had handed over a list of politicians to whom he said he had given money. But investigators would not probe all of them, "as some of Chung Tae-soo's statements lacked elements forming a crime".
Prosecutors reopened their probe into the scandal last month after the opposition attacked an earlier investigation as a whitewash.
Choi said the Chung family had used 213.6 billion won of its debt for purposes not related to "investment or the operation of Hanbo".
"The prosecution has taken steps to freeze 593.4 billion won worth of real estate and other assets of the Chung family," he said. The family had evaded taxes totalling 432.7 billion won.
Kim Hyun-chul is scheduled to testify later this month at the National Assembly's hearing on Hanbo, which is being broadcast live on television.
Next week, parliamentary hearings move to jails to question bankers and politicians in custody over the Hanbo scandal.
